--- title: "[SurvivalTree]{.doc-object-name .doc-class .doc-label .doc-label-class}" body-classes: doc-api-page page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} A survival decision tree grown with the log-rank splitting rule. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/greenwood/blob/feat-ml/greenwood/_forest.py#L358-L631){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.CLASS} ```python SurvivalTree( *, max_depth=None, min_samples_split=6, min_samples_leaf=3, max_features=None, splitter="best", engine="numpy", random_state=None ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} The tree recursively partitions subjects by covariate thresholds, at each step choosing the split that maximizes the two-sample log-rank statistic between the resulting child groups. Each leaf holds a Nelson-Aalen cumulative hazard and a Kaplan-Meier survival curve estimated from its training subjects, evaluated on the full training set's event-time grid. Prediction routes a subject to a leaf and reads off that leaf's curves; the scalar risk score is the summed cumulative hazard (ensemble mortality). A single tree is a high-variance estimator and is most useful as an interpretable building block or the base learner of a `RandomSurvivalForest`. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [max_depth]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Maximum depth of the tree. `None` grows until other stopping rules apply. [min_samples_split]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[6]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Minimum number of subjects a node must have to be eligible for splitting. [min_samples_leaf]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[3]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Minimum number of subjects required in each child of a split. [max_features]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Any]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Number of covariates considered at each split: `"sqrt"`, `"log2"`, an int, a float fraction, or `None` (all features). A random subset is drawn per node. [splitter]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [["best"]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default} : How thresholds are chosen: `"best"` (default) scans every candidate cut-point for the optimal log-rank split; `"random"` draws a single random threshold per candidate feature (the extremely-randomized-trees rule used by `ExtraSurvivalTrees`). [engine]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [["numpy"]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Compute backend for the best-split search: `"numpy"` (default) uses the deterministic vectorized path; `"numba"` uses a compiled kernel (requires the `fast` extra) that is faster on large datasets; `"auto"` uses Numba when available. The Numba path produces a statistically equivalent fit but, because it accumulates the log-rank statistic in a different order, may differ from the NumPy path in tie-breaking. [random_state]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Any]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Seed or `numpy.random.Generator` controlling the per-node feature subsampling. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} Grow a survival tree on the bundled `lung` dataset and predict a risk score: ::: {#6f6fab39 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import greenwood as gw # Load data and build a right-censored response lung = gw.load_dataset("lung", backend="pandas").dropna(subset=["ph.ecog", "ph.karno"]) y = gw.Surv.right(lung["time"], event=(lung["status"] == 2)) cols = ["age", "sex", "ph.ecog", "ph.karno", "wt.loss"] # Fit a survival tree and score the first five subjects tree = gw.SurvivalTree(max_depth=3, random_state=0).fit(y, lung[cols]) tree.predict(lung[cols])[:5] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` array([95.15345288, 95.15345288, 95.15345288, 95.15345288, 95.15345288]) ``` ::: ::: ## Methods {.doc-methods}
Name Description
fit() Fit the survival tree to a right-censored response and covariate design.
predict() Predict a risk score, survival curves, or cumulative-hazard curves.
### [fit()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} ::: {.doc-subject} Fit the survival tree to a right-censored response and covariate design. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/greenwood/blob/feat-ml/greenwood/_forest.py#L448-L505){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python fit( surv, covariates, *, data=None, _rng=None, _event_times=None, _time=None, _event=None ) ``` ::: #### Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [surv]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Surv | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A right-censored `Surv` response (built with `Surv.right()`). [covariates]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Any]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A dataframe, a 2-D array, or a right-hand-side formula string evaluated against `data`. [data]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Any]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : DataFrame used to evaluate a formula string. ::: #### Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [SurvivalTree]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The fitted estimator (for method chaining), with cached attributes such as `event_times_`, `n_features_in_`, and `feature_names_in_`. ::: ### [predict()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} ::: {.doc-subject} Predict a risk score, survival curves, or cumulative-hazard curves. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/greenwood/blob/feat-ml/greenwood/_forest.py#L569-L616){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python predict(newdata=None, *, type="risk", times=None, format=None) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} Three prediction types are available: 1. `type="risk"` (default): Ishwaran's ensemble mortality, the sum of the leaf cumulative hazard over the training event times. Higher values indicate higher risk. Returned as a 1-D NumPy array. 2. `type="survival"`: Kaplan-Meier survival probabilities $S(t \mid x)$ at `times`, one column per subject. Returned as a DataFrame. 3. `type="cumulative_hazard"`: Nelson-Aalen cumulative hazard $H(t \mid x)$ at `times`. Returned as a DataFrame. ::: #### Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [newdata]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Any]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Covariates to predict for. `None` predicts for the training subjects. [type]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [["risk"]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default} : One of `"risk"`, `"survival"`, or `"cumulative_hazard"`. [times]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Any]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Times at which to evaluate survival / cumulative hazard. Defaults to the training event times. Ignored for `type="risk"`. [format]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : DataFrame backend for curve output: `None`, `"pandas"`, `"polars"`, or `"pyarrow"`. ::: #### Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [numpy.ndarray or DataFrame]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A risk vector, or a curve frame with a `time` column and one column per subject. :::
